summary: Describes two ways to produce the public and private key pairs that BGPsec routers use to sign their routing announcements: the router can generate its own keys, or the operator can generate them and install them. The public keys are published in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure so others can check the signatures.

eli5.summary: Each router needs its own secret stamp to sign its messages. This explains two ways to make the stamp: the router makes it itself, or its owner makes it and hands it over.

questions: how are bgpsec router keys generated
router driven vs operator driven keys
how does a bgpsec router get a certificate
subtitle: Two ways to give a BGPsec router its signing keys: let the router make them, or make them for it.

tldr.problem: BGPsec routers need private keys to sign their routing announcements, and the matching public keys must be certified and published so that others can verify those signatures. The operator needs a clear way to produce and install the key pairs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a router-driven method, where the router generates its own key pair and certification request, and an operator-driven method, where the operator generates the pair and installs the private key over a protected channel. Both end with a CA-issued certificate published in the RPKI and installed on the router.
tldr.outcome: Operators can pick the method their routers support. Router-driven keying is the recommended practice when the delay of replacing a router is acceptable, and operator-driven keying supports quick hot-swapping of routers.

today: RFC 8635 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2019. The metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the description of these two BGPsec router keying methods.

sections.title: Why Routers Need Keys
sections.content:
BGPsec-speaking routers are provisioned with private keys so that they can digitally sign BGPsec announcements. To verify a signature, the public key is published as a certificate (RFC 8209) in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). RFC 8635 describes how to provision routers with these public-private key pairs.

There are two methods, and they differ in where and by whom the pair is generated. In the router-driven method the router generates its own pair. In the operator-driven method the operator generates the pair elsewhere and sends it to the router.

The document points to related specifications: RFC 8205 for BGPsec itself, RFC 8209 for the PKCS#10 certification request format, and RFC 8608 for the signature algorithms.
sections.eli5: Routers sign their messages like a person signs a letter. To sign, a router needs a secret pen, and this document explains two ways to give it one.

sections.title: Router-Driven and Operator-Driven Keys
sections.content:
The router-driven method mirrors the model used by traditional PKI subscribers: the private key never leaves trusted storage such as a Hardware Security Module (HSM). The operator tells the router to generate the key pair, build a PKCS#10 certification request (often called a CSR) and sign it with the private key. The router returns the request over the protected channel. Even if the private key cannot be extracted, that signature links a private key to a router, so the operator can verify proof of possession as required by RFC 6484.

The operator-driven method has the operator generate the pair on a management station, install the private key into the router over the protected channel, and sign the CSR itself. The RFC warns that copy-and-paste from a management station to a router can be unreliable for long texts. This method exists because of the importance of keeping networks running: when a router is replaced, the same private key can be installed in the new router, which causes minimal downtime compared with the normal RPKI procedures to propagate a new key, which can take a day or longer to converge.

Operators may use either method as the platform supports. Prudent security practice recommends router-generated keying if the delay in replacing a router (or router engine) is acceptable.

An operator-driven private key SHOULD be wrapped in a PKCS#8 Asymmetric Key Package (RFC 5958), further encapsulated in CMS SignedData and signed with the operator's End Entity private key. The router SHOULD verify that signature.
sections.eli5: Either the router invents its own secret pen and never shows it to anyone, or the owner makes the pen and carefully hands it to the router. The second way lets you give a new router the same pen as the old one.

sections.title: From Setup to an Installed Certificate
sections.content:
Whichever method is chosen, the operator first establishes a protected channel between the management system and the router. It must prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery, and provide mutual authentication. How it is set up is router-specific; the RFC assumes an SSH-protected command line. An initial leap of faith is unavoidable because the router has no keying material yet, so a direct physical connection is safer than a network connection.

In setup, the operator installs the RPKI Trust Anchor's Certificate in the router and configures the Autonomous System (AS) number and the BGP Identifier to be used in the router certificate. If the operator chooses not to use unique per-router certificates, a BGP Identifier of 0 MAY be used. The PKCS#10 request does not carry the AS number or BGP Identifier, so the operator sends them to the CA along with the CSR.

The CA validates the request, certifies the key, publishes the certificate in the Global RPKI and returns it to the operator in a PKCS#7 certs-only message, SHOULD include the certificate chain below the trust anchor. The operator provisions that message into the router. The router SHOULD check that the public key matches its stored private key, and that the certificate validates back to the installed trust anchor, and SHOULD tell the operator the result.

A router should not talk to the CA directly in the basic methods, because the CA would have no way to authenticate it. The operator, who knows the router is genuine, mediates.
sections.eli5: First you build a safe tunnel to the router. Then the router (or you) writes a request for an official ID card, a trusted office issues the card, and the router checks the card really matches its secret pen.

sections.title: Advanced Deployment for Capable Routers
sections.content:
More PKI-capable routers can lighten the operator's burden. Typically they carry preinstalled manufacturer-driven certificates (for example IEEE 802.1AR) or preinstalled Pre-Shared Keys, plus PKI-enrollment functionality and a transport protocol such as Enrollment over Secure Transport (RFC 7030). The preinstalled key material is used to authenticate the router when the protected channel is first set up.

The operator's work then shifts to three tasks: securely telling the CA about the router's authentication material (at least the AS number, BGP Identifier and key material), enabling the router to reach the CA (possibly through firewalls and NATs), and ensuring a cryptographic chain of custody from the manufacturer.

Because the router talks to the CA directly, the operator does not fetch the PKCS#10 or return the PKCS#7. The router should still perform its certificate checks, and SHOULD automatically re-contact the CA later to renew its certificate.
sections.eli5: Some routers come with a factory ID badge. They can walk up to the ID office themselves, so their owner has less running around to do.

sections.title: Validity, Rollover, Revocation and Replacement
sections.content:
Key management continues for as long as the router runs BGPsec. The router must always sign with a valid private key, so the operator must make sure the router always has an unexpired certificate. The RFC lists ways to track expiry (router notifications, calendar reminders, CA warnings, or automated tracking), advises warnings well in advance and recommends notifying additional operators in the same organization.

Rollover: routers that support multiple private keys can obtain and distribute the new key and certificate before the operational key expires. Details are in RFC 8634.

Revocation: the operator uses the RPKI CA system to place the router's certificate on the Certificate Revocation List and to re-key the router. Keeping the router speaking BGPsec is the ideal goal; if that is impractical, disabling BGPsec is likely preferred to taking the router offline.

Replacement: to allow quick replacement without updating public keys in the RPKI, routers SHOULD allow the private BGPsec key to be inserted via a protected channel such as SSH, NETCONF or SNMP. A router MAY allow export of the key after generation, but this SHOULD be paired with a way to set the key to a permanent non-exportable state.
sections.eli5: An ID card runs out, so you have to renew it before that happens. If the secret pen is stolen you cancel the card and get a new one, and when a router breaks the new one can be given the old pen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines no protocols, so in some sense it introduces no new security considerations, but it relies on many other protocols whose security considerations should be consulted. It repeats three bootstrapping issues:

  • Key pair generation: mistakes are catastrophic; all key pairs MUST be generated from a good source of non-deterministic random input (RFC 4086).
  • Private key protection at rest: all private keys MUST be protected securely when stored.
  • Private key protection in transit: transport security is strongly RECOMMENDED, and it SHOULD be at least as good as the strength of the BGPsec key.

The revocation status of the CA certificate installed on the router is rarely checked, so the operator MUST ensure that the installed CA certificate is valid. Appendix A says the protected channel should be at least as strong as the 128-bit strength of the BGPsec keys, which rules out export grade crypto and Triple-DES.
sections.eli5: A secret pen is only useful if nobody else gets it. So make it with truly random luck, lock it away, and only carry it in a locked box.
